entities.name: Châtelperronian
entities.label: Timeframe
entities.summary:
The Châtelperronian, an archaeological culture flourishing between approximately 36,000 and 31,000 BCE, represents a pivotal and fiercely debated chapter in the transition from the Middle to the Upper Paleolithic in Western Europe. Characterized by a distinctive lithic industry featuring elongated blades and bone tools, it is primarily associated with the last Neanderthal populations, particularly in regions spanning France and northern Spain. Its significance lies in its unique blend of Mousterian (Middle Paleolithic) technological traditions with innovations previously attributed solely to anatomically modern humans, challenging long-held assumptions about Neanderthal cognitive capabilities and cultural development.

Key achievements of the Châtelperronian include the production of specialized tools such as the Châtelperronian point, a knife-like blade with a blunted back, often crafted from flint. More remarkably, sites like the Grotte du Renne at Arcy-sur-Cure in France have yielded personal ornaments, including perforated animal teeth, ivory rings, and bone pendants, alongside evidence of bone and antler working. These artifacts signify a complexity in symbolic thought and technological prowess that parallels early Upper Paleolithic Homo sapiens cultures like the Aurignacian, suggesting either independent innovation by Neanderthals or cultural exchange with incoming modern human populations.
